utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Unfortunately, my absence took 25 minutes more than expected. I do understand that this was perhaps an unpleasant surprise for all those waiting. Apologies for that. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before I start, Mr. President, I just want to correct the record. At T11450, yesterday in the course of legal submissions, I referred to two records of interviews, tendered by the Defence as D902 and D904. The second document as recorded as "D8904." I just wanted to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The record is hereby corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document 6090 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, can I ask, while that document is being brought up, if you could turn to paragraph 38 of your supplementary statement. And at paragraph 38, you refer to a document and you say as follows: "I am now shown a copy of a special report dated 27 June 2002 sent by military police crime investigation section to me: "According to this report, the military police was investigating suspects in relation to the killings in Varivode and Gosic, which included a suspect; namely, Goran Vunic. The investigation included an intention to obtain details of the weapons allocated to individual members of the units, and also to seize the weapons from a military unit for purposes of ballistic analysis, with bullet casings recovered from the scene of the crime in connection with killings in Gosic. The investigation was prevented from being carried out by the commander of the military police company, Nenad Mrkota. I recall this matter and the material submitted in relation to this. "The investigating military police officer, Simic, will be in a better position to offer more information on this matter. These materials were submitted to me at my request. I believe if this investigation had been carried out as planned, the real perpetrators of this crime may have been brought to trial. As far as I know, Goran Vunic was always mentioned in the capacity of a suspect in relation to this case. I am not aware of him being considered as an informant or a witness in this case." Mr. Zganjer, can you just look at the document on the screen and tell us - and this is, in fact, the document you identified in paragraph 38 - who exactly, and I'd like you to state the exact designation or person who has sent this special report to you. And if you could perhaps look at the top of the document and then at the end, the signature. Let us know when you want the document to be moved to the next page, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I would like to correct an error in my supplementary statement. 15 January 1995 is mentioned here as the date of my birth, and it is an error. I was born in 1955, not in 1995. Now I am ready to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mistake in the Croatian version of your statement, Mr. Zganjer, because in the English version, which you have signed, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let not spend too much time on that. It is clear to everyone that you were not born in 1995. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, can you answer my question. My question was: Could you please look at this document, look at the top of the document and the signatory, and tell us the exact designation of the person who has sent you this special report. Do you want to see the second page?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that I, indeed, received this document that I mentioned in paragraph 38 of my supplementary statement. The document, as far as I remember, and I believe that I remember it well, was personally brought to me by the chief of the department of the crime prevention military police. If you show me the second page of this report, it is possible that I will be able to give you his name very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: While we're going to the second page, would you confirm --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could go down on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It was brought to me personally by Mr. Ante Glaven, the chief of the crime administration of the military police. He brought me the document with the enclosures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: If I -- do you agree with me, Mr. Zganjer, if I mention his full designation as follows: Chief of the military police service department of the military crime police within the administration for intelligence and security or the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you ever so slightly. He was the chief of the administration of the crime prevention military police, Major Ante Glavan. The addition where you mention intelligence and security, that would be a special part of the Ministry of Defence, a special service within the Ministry of Defence. Here, we're talking about the military police; to be more specific, the administration of the crime prevention military police at the time headed by Major Ante Glavan. In other words, this document is not directly connected with the security system of the Ministry of Defence. This document is the product of the work of the crime prevention department, within the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Zganjer. I don't disagree with you. I just wanted to point out --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Does that unit come within ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: ... come within the administration for intelligence and security of the Ministry of Defence? What I want to know is whether his unit also comes within the larger section of intelligence and security of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the administration for security and intelligence in the heading of this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and its letterhead. But as far as I know, in the Ministry of Defence, yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's all right. And if we go to the document itself at paragraph 1, it reads as follows: "Pursuant to your demand ..." -- If you could follow the document, Mr. Zganjer, the on the screen: "Pursuant to your demand to undertake all necessary actions from the reference, military police crime department of the military police service, continued with data and documentation collection. So we collected the documentation in connection conduct of members of miliary police company of the 72nd Sibenik Military Police Battalion, during the operation action Varivode conducted in October 1995 by MUP, Ministry of Interior of Republic of Croatia, crime police, in cooperation with members of the military police upon the request of the county public prosecutor in Zadar, on the occasion of serious crimes committed in Gosic and Varivode." The next paragraph reads: "Documentation ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, as you continue to read, apparently you're reading from another translation than ours. Differences are perhaps not that substantial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're reading is not we see as the translation. So, therefore, I'm wondering whether you are orienting yourself on a different translation than you have uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I have the revised translation it seems, but I will read off the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The version on the screen is unrevised. So if there is a revised version, I have no problem with you reading. Then, of course, the revised translation should be in uploaded in e-court and not that you are in possession of a revised portion; whereas, you ask us to look at an unrevised version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President. It was my mistake. I didn't realise what was on e-court was the unrevised portion. I thought it was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thinking about it, when you see it on your screen, it says "unrevised," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. President. I was just following my hard copy, but I didn't -- I just want to address the witness, so I will go to the unrevised version. Then, later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if you say the revised portion is available to you, of course the witness sees the original and, therefore, is not bothered that much by the translation we are looking at and the translation you're reading at this moment. Mr. Misetic was on his feet, but he is not anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have in front of me the unrevised version myself. I'm checking with my case manager to see if we were disclosed the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll let you know in a minute. I'm just checking with -- the revisions have been going on as we speak, Mr. President, so I don't know at what stage -- this was, you know, printed by me last night. So let me give you an answer in a minute. In the meantime, may I proceed on this with the unrevised version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I would say, then, please continue on the basis of the revised version because you started reading from that. The witness looks at an original; and then, at a later stage, we will have to check whether there are any substantial difference between the two. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: The next paragraph, Mr. Zganjer, reads: "Documentation collected is related to Goran Vunic who was supposed to be criminally processed due to reasonable doubt that, that at time in question, he was at the locations of the crimes committed in Gosic and Varivode. And pursuant to injunction of the county court in Zadar, he was supposed to be criminally processed. Military court in Split gave the injunction for investigative procedures against him, but all the procedures were stopped pursuant to order of the then-Captain Nenad Mrkota, commander of the military police company in Sibenik, now civilian, about which Lieutenant Damir Simic, head of military police crime department of the Military Police Company in Sibenik, mad an Official Note. An interview was conducted with Damir Simic about the circumstances mentioned before, and a record on statement taken was also made." I just want to, before I ask you the question, Mr. Zganjer, take you to a couple of more points on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're just going through an exercise of reading what is in a document, I think that's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the propriety of reading depends on the question that follows. Therefore, Ms. Mahindaratne, if you would just read to seek confirmation or if you are reading because the witness should be reminded on what in the letter, so as to be able to answer other questions, then, of course, there's nothing wrong. But it should not be an exercise in which you seek either further details or substantially the same as we find in the document already. So if you would please keep in mind when you decide whether or not you decide to continue to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I just wanted to remind the witness, as well as to place a foundation for my next question. I wasn't going through a reading exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could, Mr. Registrar, if you could turn to the next page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: At the paragraph numbered 4, it reads: "According to information collected in the course of the crime investigation, and according to the documentation submitted in the attachment of the special report, it is evidence that Nenad Mrkota had information of certain circumstances in connection to the crimes committed and potential perpetrates. And through his acts, he directly influenced the treatment of the persons during the examination, especially regarding the treatment of Goran Vunic. Thereby, he committed a criminal offence. "Also, there is suspicion that Nenad Mrkota by his acts and instructions influenced or personally committed the crimes of destroying or covering evidence related to the criminal offence committed in Gosic and Varivode." Then there is further details of what has been found out, and there is -- you're reported as to what further steps are being taken with regard to this matter. And paragraph 3, under the section numbered 4, reads: "In accordance with the above mentioned, we believe it is necessary to conduct special measures of control and technical interception of the telephone calls; namely, equipment for technical communication on distance according to Article 180."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on the English, we have to move to the next page, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Registrar, if we could move to the next one. Yes. Thank you. And if you could go --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: "Law on Criminal Procedure which should cover the following persons who have information or are in relation to the crimes committed in Gosic and Varivode, and there are persons named there: Civilians Nenad Mrkota, Ivan Mikulandra, Bosko Ramljak, Josip Juras, and military staff Colonel Mihalj Budimir and Colonel Miro Primorac." Mr. Zganjer, let me first ask you this question: Who is the person who is referred to as Colonel Mihalj Budimir there? Do you know what his position was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Mihalj Budimir. Actually, his name rings a bell. I believe that he was, in 1982 and thereafter, the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police in Split. I know that because from April or May 1992 to May 1993, I was the deputy military prosecutor in Sibenik. I don't know what the case was after 1993, whether he remained in that position and for how long, whether he was still the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police in Split. I believe that he was, but I don't know for how long. I wouldn't be able to tell you, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the beginning of 1993, or rather, in June 1993, I left the prosecutor's office and became the state attorney in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Now, are you able to tell Court as to what the outcome of this investigation was, with regard to the conduct of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, particularly the conduct of Nenad Mrkota, you know, preventing the investigation that was being conducted against Goran Vunic? Was there a final result in that investigation that is reported in this special report to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this report, as I have already told you, towards the end of June 2003. I know that I had contacts and exchanges with the officials of the military police and that we spoke primarily about the situation at hand and whether we could, seven years after the incidents in Varivode and Gosic, find the weapons of the 113th Brigade of the Croatian army of its scouting squad; and if we could, whether we could subject the weapons to a ballistic expertise in order to establish whether any of those weapons that had been issued to the members of the 113 Brigade, whether they had been used to fire at people in Gosic and Varivode. I would like to emphasise that in the place where civilians had been killed in Gosic and Varivode, some bullet casings were found; in other words, when I received this special report, our efforts was primarily focussed on the attempts to locate the weapons and to carry out ballistic investigation with a view to establishing, perhaps, that some of these weapons had been used to fire from in Gosic and Varivode. As far as I can remember at this moment, and it was seven years ago, we made several attempts to locate the weapons. Some of the weapons, as far as I can remember, had been conserved. Some of the weapons were found. I was informed that some of the weapons that had been found did undergo ballistic expertise. While I was the county state attorney in Sibenik, I did not receive those ballistic results that had been carried out. I stopped being the county state attorney on the 15th of September, 2002, and moved to Zagreb to assume a different duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, just to correct the record, you said that you received this special report towards the end of June 2003. I think you meant to say 2002. I just wanted to correct that on the record. Now was Goran Vunic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Do you know within which unit Goran Vunic was during 1995 at the time that he was being investigated? I'm not talking about the subunit, but, generally, the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to lack of foundation for reasons that will be more clear in cross-examination, Your Honour. But if Ms. Mahindaratne can establish that Mr. Vunic was a subject of an investigation in 1995 and when, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think I have tendered enough and more documents which shows that Mr. Goran Vunic was being investigated with regard to the killings incident in Gosic. I tendered P970, P971, the document that is on the screen now shows it. I don't know what else Mr. Misetic expects me to tender to establish that Mr. Vunic was being investigated in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is an attachment, I believe, to this exhibit which Ms. Mahindaratne is going do tender. I withdraw the objection, but I think you will see it more clearly when the attachment is brought forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you do not mind that the Chamber, on the basis of the series of numbers, cannot immediately understand. If there would be no foundation, we'll find out. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, my question was: Do you know the brigade in which Mr. Goran Vunic was at the time he was being investigated in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the Court will allow me to answer the question after the previous exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could tell us the brigade in which Mr. Goran Vunic was in 1995. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, Mr. Goran Vunic was a member of the 113th Brigade of the Croatian army, and I also remember another very concrete detail with regard to his position. I believe that he was the commander of one of the squads of the scouting company of the 113th Brigade of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P1062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1062 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may have I document P970, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, just for the record, I heard of no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, have you seen this document before? Let us know when you want to go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be so kind and show me the next page of the document. I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Was it sent to you with the special report that we looked at previously?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 1, the paragraph which is numbered 1, it reads -- this is a note compiled by senior Lieutenant Damir Simic. It reads: "Goran Vunic, son of Ante," and the details are given, "member of the 113th Infantry Brigade, for the following reason, after Operation Storm, on an undetermined day in August 1995, together with two other as of yet unidentified men, he has shot and killed Gojko Lezajic in the courtyard of his house in Gosici. The neighbours have buried the body at the local cemetery, (statements given by Savo Letunica and Milan Letunica)." I read that to you because it is relevant to the next document that I will call up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have, Mr. Registrar, document number 6091.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Now, if I could take to you paragraph 39 of your supplementary statement, Mr. Zganjer. If I could ask you to look at paragraph 39 of your supplementary statement, you say: "I am now shown a copy of letter dated 23 October 1995 sent by the Zadar county public prosecutor to Zadar-Knin police administration regarding the criminal proceedings in the Varivode, Gosic, Zrmanja case. "In this case, one of the suspects in the killing incident in Gosic of Gojko Lezajic was Goran Vunic. By this letter, the Zadar county public prosecutor has directed the Zadar-Knin police to investigate the matter. I am familiar with this document." Now, was this letter also enclosed with the special report that we looked at earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 1 of this letter, the paragraph numbered 1, it again says, and I will not -- there is an handwritten note, "Goran Vunic," and then it starts: "Vunic," and there is a blank of a place, "Cista Velika, now a refugee in Vodice (shaven head with a tuft on top of his head resembling a bird's nest) on an undetermined date in August 1995, after Operation Storm, in concert with two other as yet unidentified persons, used fire-arms and killed Gojko Lezajic in the courtyard of his house in Gosic, whom the villagers later buried in the local cemetery (statements of Savo Letunica and Milan Letunica)." Now, in the Croatian version, the name Goran Vunic is handwritten text. Do you know who wrote that there in hand writing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote that by their hand. Perhaps it's the person who signed this request to the Zadar-Knin police administration. It was done in 1995 while the area of Gosici was within the jurisdiction of that state attorney's office, and it was done in 1995 by that state attorney's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Now, did you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this document on the basis that Goran Vunic's name is handwritten on this document, when you received it with your -- as an enclosure with the special report we looked at a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the question as to what counsel means by "authenticity." Is that authentically that somebody wrote by hand a name, or is she suggesting that the name underneath the blanked-out portion is the same as the name written in hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could include these observations in his answer. If he says that he has doubts as to the authenticity, to explain to us what he meant; but if he had no doubts, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, could you respond to my question please, and the question was whether you had any doubts as to the authenticity of this document, and you could factor in the issues raised by Mr. Misetic, when you received this document enclosed with the special report that was sent to you. That is a document we looked at a little while ago, dated 27 June 2002.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that what we have here is an unusual intervention in the text of a memo that the state attorney's office sent to the competent police structure. However, there was no reason for me to doubt that this was Goran Vunic. Why was that? Well, in addition to this document, I received others from which it followed that the military police, in 1995, had a certain amount of suspicion against precisely Goran Vunic. A moment ago, you showed to me a document signed by police officer, Mr. Damir Simic, where, beyond doubt, one of the suspects involved was Goran Vunic. This individual is mentioned in this document as well. The document is dated 23rd of October, 1993; whereas, the one you showed to me a moment ago, signed by Mr. Damir Simic, was dated the 25th of October, 1995, if I'm not mistaken. These were two separate documents produced two days apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, and I suggest that we MFI the exhibit. The Defence will be in cross-examination showing the witness the original letter, in which the name in point 1 is, in fact, not Goran Vunic that was sent by the county prosecutor' office. We were provided with the original by the state attorney's office in Croatia, I'm surprised that OTP didn't ask for the original, but we will be exploring this in cross-examination. I suggest we MFI it and let the Trial Chamber decide how we should deal with the exhibit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just place on the record, that a comparison of this document and P970, which we looked at a little while ago, I think clearly indicates that the person referred in the two paragraphs are one and the same, because the details are exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the original document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see for the time being. Ms. Mahindaratne expresses that she has no doubt as to the authenticity of this document, whatever that may mean. Mr. Misetic says that he has another original, well, still to be considered. There could be even two authenticate documents, the one not exactly the same as the other one. Authenticity, of course, should be interpreted when talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- context. We'll, for the time being, Ms. Mahindaratne, we'll mark this document for identification. A final decision on admission in view of any authenticity issue raised or any other issue raised will be decided by the Chamber after we have seen all the information the parties want to present to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me just state, for the record, we will, in fact, be going step by step through the investigation up to the point of this letter, and exploring matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Misetic, the Chamber will see how you will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne -- no. First, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1063, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1063 keeps that status. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, can I take you to paragraph 45 of your supplementary statement. In paragraph 45, and that is quite a lengthy paragraph, I will only read a section that is starting from line 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Starting from line 7 you say -- you refer to the Varivode, Gosici, and Zrmanja case, and you say: "At the completion of the trial, the accused were acquitted of the charges of murder relating to the killings in Varivode and Gosic, and Ivica Petric was convicted of the killing incident in Zrmanja and sentenced to six years in prison." Then you give further details of it, and you say: "However, the Supreme Court set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the Zadar county court for retrial. Then with the territorial change, the case came within the jurisdiction of the Sibenik county court; and as county state prosecutor, I was responsible for the case. "Having taken over the case, I analysed the evidence and established that there was no reliable evidence to proceed against those accused who had been indicted in the case. I discussed this with the state attorney for Croatia and his deputies, and received his approval to dismiss the case against the five persons who had been indicted. I'm not aware of any other persons being tried for the crimes after that. I believe if the military police officer Simic had been allowed to carry out the investigation, including ballistic investigation in October 1995 as planned, the real perpetrators of the crime could have been identified." Now, as a state prosecutor in charge of the case, did you examine all the criminal and investigative files relating to the Varivode, Gosic, Zrmanja cases before you arrived at your conclusion that there was no reliable evidence to proceed against the five persons who had been indicted in the case which was tried?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Zrmanja, which you referred to in your question, were a case that where a final decision was rendered. I received a file which concerned the killing of civilians in Gosic and Varivode. I assure you that I examined the case file carefully and thoroughly. It was not a small matter to approach the state attorney and tell him that in that case, I did not see any reasonable grounds indicating that the individuals mentioned therein were the perpetrators. I sifted through the matters involved in the case carefully because I was resolute in my intention that charges should be dropped against the person who is were accused of not less than 17 civilians killed in Gosic and Varivode. Seven were killed in Gosic and nine in Varivode. That would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Zganjer. Now, in one of those materials that you examined -- you said that you examined the case files for Varivode and Gosic thoroughly. Now in any one of those materials, was there any reason recorded as to why the investigation against Goran Vunic had been stopped by Nenad Mrkota?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One matter needs clarification on that score. There was a case file which referred to the cases of Gosic and Varivode, which, once the jurisdiction changed, was transferred from the Zadar county court to the Sibenik county court. I was given a part of the state attorney's case file concerning Gosic and Varivode. I thoroughly examined and studied the evidence contained in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Vunic, as far as that case file is concerned, and I stress the case file, was not mentioned as a person who would be under suspicion this way or the other. When is it that the name of Goran Vunic ultimately emerges? When I decided to desist the criminal prosecution of those suspects, the following question arose: If, as I was deeply convinced, those persons were not the perpetrators, who was it that killed the 17 individuals? At that point, for a state attorney, the proceedings against those accused ended; however, the pre-trial proceedings commenced of establishing who the perpetrators were. The results of that -- of those particular proceedings, the pre-trial proceedings, led me to learn in 2002 that, for certain reasons, the commander of the military police company in Sibenik, Nenad Mrkota, had obstructed the activity of the military police of Damir Simic. It was at that point that the suspicion arose, which made me believe that Goran Vunic could be the possible perpetrator of the events in Gosic and Varivode. Based on the information I can see on the screen here, the authenticity of which is something that the Defence doubts. Goran Vunic became a suspect for the competent state attorney's office back in 1995 and I received the case file in 1999, when the change of jurisdiction occurred; and at that point, I took adequate actions and measures aimed at finding, identifying the perpetrators of the act. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Yes, you were, Mr. Zganjer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have, again, dealing with a translation problem as it regards to the "pre-criminal" proceedings, which has been translated as the "pre-trial." We solved the problem yesterday, but, again, the transcript for today is all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer, and I have an only a few questions. Yesterday, we discussed about the investigation conducted by members of the Sibenik-Knin crime police into the Grubori incident on your instructions. Now, if I could take to you paragraph 19 of your supplementary statement, you referred to one of the investigators, named Josko Ferara. You say that you went with him, you visited the village of Grubori, in order to get an impression of the area to yourself. Now, also yesterday, you mentioned that you had a meeting and discussions with the investigators; and to be precise, I'll read exactly what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is, for the record, at transcript number 11.512.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: You say: "There is an conversation that I held with the police officers who were involved in the criminal proceedings in this case. I made a note of that conversation on the cover of my case files." I'm referring here to the Grubori investigation, Mr. Zganjer. Now my question is: Did you know the police officers who were conducting the investigation, the investigation initiated by you, in 2001? When I say ask you whether you knew them, I'm asking did you know them professionally. I'm not -- not referring to personal contact.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to my supplementary statement at paragraph 19. I knew the police officer Josko Ferara personally, as I did many other police officers from the police administration of Sibenik-Knin. I worked as a state attorney for 24 years, holding various positions in Sibenik; and by virtue of my position, I knew many police officers. It was only natural. If you're asking me about the note that I made in my file --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you answered my question. Now, you said you have worked with the Sibenik-Knin crime police for a while when you worked as a Sibenik county state prosecutor. Now, do you have any reason to consider that when these officers conducted the interviews, in relation to the witnesses of the Grubori event on your instructions, that they conducted those interviews properly within the -- in accordance with the Croatian law, preserving the rights of those who were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the interviews conducted by policemen with persons who had certain knowledge of the events in Grubori were done professionally and properly, in full respect of the dignity and the integrity of citizens. At the time when I was the county state attorney, I had never had occasion to hear that such interviews were conducted in a manner that would be inappropriate or rough.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Now, we discussed a number of records of interviews yesterday, and also you have examined a number of records of interviews in -- by your supplementary statement. Do you consider the records of interviews that you looked at and referred to in your supplementary statement, as well as we looked at yesterday, to reflect an accurate record of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm objecting, Your Honour, at this point, because I really think that this witness cannot possibly answer that question. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe, as a prosecutor, prosecutor, he has a knowledge of the manner and the methods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. But that is a different matter because you're now focussing on specific documents. Let me perhaps put a question to the witness. Did you ever have the experience, by receiving complaints or by receiving any other information or through personal observation, did you ever have the experience that what police officers did write down in relation to those interviews was not in accordance with, was not reflecting what the interviewed persons had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about the notes as the result of interviews that the police conducted with citizens who had certain knowledge of the events in Grubori, then I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in general. I'm not focussing at this moment on any reports on Grubori, but I want to know whether in your experience, as a state attorney, whether ever, through your personal observation, through other information, through complaints by whatever means, that you were confronted with the situation where this information or this observation or these complaints raised serious doubts as to whether the police, in their Official Notes, had written down something different from what the interviewed person would have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had such experience. There were cases when citizens were summoned by the investigating judge to testify, and they expressed their reservations in respect of what was contained in the notes of the interviews conducted with these persons by police officers. In my career, I oftentimes processed police officers for their abuse of position. I processed such events where the actions of police officers crossed the boundaries of their duty or where force was applied, in violation of the rules governing precisely the situations in which a police officer may use force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about incorrect reflection of the interview, not as a result of force, but just by, well, putting something down on paper which is not in line, is not reflecting what that person had told this police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were such cases, too. If you will allow me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a clarification. How does a police officer in the Republic of Croatia compile an Official Note? He listens to a person, writes down notes in his notebook reflecting what the person says, and then he uses his notes to draft an Official Note. The Official Note is not read out to citizens. That particular citizen will not sign the Official Note either. For that reason, the note is only a piece of information, and it can by no means be a piece of evidence. The procedure of drafting the Official Note, which I've just described, allows the police officer to interpret some parts of the statement he hears from the citizen more freely, and to then put it into an Official Note. That is why, under our system, this note is always regarded as a piece of information and not as a piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained in your last answer that there is some latitude in interpreting what a witness said and then put it on paper, and that it is not read back to him. Did you also experience that the police officer did not interpret the words in a different way, but put down on paper something almost entirely different from what the witness said? For example, if the witness would say, "I saw Mr. A or I saw a person driving in a Mercedes," that the police officer would put down on paper, the witness said that he saw person B and that person B was driving in a Renault, rather than a Mercedes. Did you experience this apparently intentional distortion of what an interviewed person said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were such cases in my many years of practice, where a person questioned by an investigating judge or a judge during a hearing, would state something that was materially different from what was stated in the note compiled by a police officer. Was the witness stating the truth in his addressing the court or was the truth contained in the Official Note is something that can be debated. However, we, as professionals in Croatia, find the statements stated by the person before an investigating judge or a judge in court as the material statement, and then the Official Note is excluded from -- the Official Note is excluded from the file, and it cannot be part of evidence ever, but there were such discrepancies in statements. I'm speaking in general terms and in terms of my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do see and hear from you what consequences would be drawn from inconsistent statements given at various moments under the law of evidence. A very specific question: Were there ever cases known to you in which it could be established clearly that the police officer intentionally had written down something quite different from what the interviewed person had said? Let me be clear on this matter. I see the point you make, that a statement given to the police and interviewed or examined on the same matter at a later stage by someone else can show an inconsistency, which, as you rightly observed, raises the issue of when did the person tell the truth. But there is even one question earlier that is whether, at all, it was put on paper what he said, whether the truth or not. Now, is there any case known to you or was there any practice known to you in which police officers would intentionally or with gross violation of their duty to put down on paper what an interviewed person had said, that they nevertheless did write down something quite different from what he said or what he told these police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that I am not aware of a case when a policeman would intentionally and maliciously distort the contents of a person's statement. I believe it will not come as a surprise if I tell you that the suspects' statements would often appear different than the statements that the same persons provided to the police officials. When they came into court, their statement would differ greatly. Those statements would rarely be in collision if the statements were provided to the police and to the court by civilians appearing as witnesses. It is only logical that a person, when appearing before the investigating judge says, "Yes, I said it before the police because they had slapped me a couple of times, so I confessed everything. But now that I'm appearing before you, I have to deny everything that I said before to the police." So when we're talking about the category of suspects, it happens more often that their statements given before the police contradict what they want to say before the judge. When we're talking about civilians providing witness statements, then the controversy happens less often; and if it does, the -- it is of milder character. I don't know if I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just rise to my feet because I'm puzzled by the position taken by the Prosecution here. We all have an obligation to put our case to the witness. With respect to this witness, when it comes to the Varivode, Gosici incident, I believe the Prosecution is not putting on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it appropriate to discuss the matter in the presence of the witness? Let me try to be very practical at this moment. If it has to be put to the witness, then, of course, he should hear. But if for whatever reason it is not appropriate to put it to the witness, he should not hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It should be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, it should be put to him at the end of this discussion, but not already through the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I would still like to make my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to that. Ms. Mahindaratne, very, practically first of all, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Only two more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more questions. Then could I ask you, Mr. Zganjer, do you speak and/or understand English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, he does, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zganjer, do you speak or understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand quite a lot; however, if I were asked to say something in English, it would not be as easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I had not invite to you do so. It's just whether you were able to follow major parts of a brief discussion we might have. Could I ask you to leave the courtroom just for a second, so that the Chamber will listen to what Mr. Misetic wants to say, and then we'd like to see you back soon, for the last two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was about to suggest that I could finish it with one question, and then we could have the discussion, but then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I take it that Mr. Misetic insists on fairness to the witness. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's fairness to the witness, but it is also putting the case -- what is the Prosecution's case. I rise because, on the one hand, they're putting on a case, with respect to the Varivode and Gosic murders, that the accused in that case confessed to the police, which was the basis of why they were tried in the first place, confessions to the police. This witness now has testified that there was no reasonable basis whatsoever for him to continue to pursue these individuals with the confession in the file from these individuals given to the police. Then, with respect to Grubori, Ms. Mahindaratne rises to now get the witness to say that police statements given by people, he has never encountered a situation where they were not credible. It should be put to the witness how he explains, on the one hand, not even pursuing a criminal case with confessions in the file; and, on the other hand, if she wishes to have him say that statements given in the context of the Grubori case, however, or otherwise, were reliable, then how could have testified earlier that there was no reasonable basis to continue to pursue the people who had confessed in the Varivode incident. I think the Prosecution has an obligation to be -- to put their case to the witness; and to the extent there is any inconsistency what the witness has said with respect to how he handled the cases, that should be resolved on their questioning, and not to leave that somehow they want to get Grubori documents in, so the system functioned perfectly with respect to the to the police. With respect to Varivode, it was some conspiracy where the individuals were beaten into providing confessions to the police. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know from where Mr. Misetic got that it was the Prosecution's thesis or the basis that the Varivode suspects were beaten, or the confessions. The entire -- we, the Prosecution, has not led much evidence or it has not been one of the scheduled incidents in this case. The issue about Varivode, Gosici, and Zrmanja came up because with regard to the evidence that was led through Damir Simic, and this witness, about the previous suspects not being properly investigated, that was the issue. Then, in the course of cross-examination of witness Simic, Mr. Misetic tendered an excerpt of a judgement, on the basis that it was an excerpt of a judgement from the Varivode case. He went on record saying that Goran Vunic, in fact, was -- that Goran Vunic testified in the Varivode, Gosici, Zrmanja cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Transcript reference please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Transcript reference would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can cut this short. We've gone back and forth on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I can read transcript from ... [Overlapping speakers] ... T10325 to T10327.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Read out what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With your permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it you're inviting Ms. Mahindaratne to read out what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The portion particularly where I said he testified in the Varivode, Gosici cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could please at least observe in every respect politeness instead of giving orders inviting other parties to do something. If there is any need for any order to do a thing, you may address this Bench, and the Bench will, if that is appropriate, issue an order for one of the parties to do what the other party wishes that part to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you wish me to read this transcript? I have it exactly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Misetic invited you to do so. So if you follow that invitation, then I don't have to express myself on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Mr. Misetic's question: "This is now on the screen, sir. This is a judgement concerning the case that you had investigated, and we've translated certain excerpts. In the judgement, you can see that Goran Vunic subsequently became a witness in that case and gave evidence as a witness. Were you aware, subsequent to October 1995, that Goran Vunic became a witness in the case that you had investigated?" "A. No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Okay." Then there is a conversation with the Court. "Q. Are you aware whether Goran Vunic at any point became a protected witness in the investigation?" Then I object: "Mr. President, objection. I think the witness has answered this question several times in examination-in-chief and just now." Then Court rules. Then, again, the question is asked: "Mr. Simic, let me ask you the question again: At any point in time, did you receive any information that Goran Vunic was a protected witness in that case? "A. No, I never received such information."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I respond, Mr. President, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe Chambers was copied on my e-mail. My position was that he testified in OA Varivode, which was the operative investigation. I have already advised Ms. Mahindaratne, if she felt something was unclear, we could put it on the record. So, to the extent it was unclear, I put it on the record, but it doesn't change the position of why 843 was tendered. Moreover, we are now far afield from what my objection is. It is patently absurd that somehow these questions are being led because of a question I put to him. The issue is that it is the Prosecution's position, from the evidence they first led with Damir Simic, that there was a cover-up in the Varivode case, that she has proceeded now to take Mr. Mrkota, Mr. Budimir, several other people in a public session, and essentially accuse them of a cover-up in the Varivode case, which I think when you see the cross-examination in my position, is that there was no foundation for those allegations. But, more importantly, the issue is they are claiming that there is some sort of a cover-up. This witness had confessions from people in the file that had nothing to do with Mr. Mrkota, Mr. Goran Vunic, Mr. Budimir, et cetera. So the Prosecution has to take a position, either there was a cover-up with Mr. Vunic and Mr. Mrkota in the Varivode case, in which case the confessions in the file were not accurate; or, the confessions in the file were accurate, this witness failed in his responsibility to continue to prosecute the case, and the allegation of a cover-up is either not true or at least is irrelevant to the issue of the fact that the individuals who confessed still should have been prosecuted. However we look at it, we go back to the first issue, which is how do you justify saying the confessions in the Varivode case are not valid, while at the same time saying that every statement given to the police is accurate, or should be generally to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic apparently sees inconsistency in your approach of the matter. Now, I leave for a moment my doubts whether there was also an obligation for the Prosecution to put inconsistencies in their approach. Could you, first of all, explain to us what, in your view, on the matter raised by Mr. Misetic, what the position of the Prosecution is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no inconsistency at all. The issue is that Mr. Misetic has confused facts. The witness's testimony is that five persons -- those five persons did not include Goran Vunic of who were indicted. The matter was tried, and they were acquitted, and the case came back for retrial when he examined the entire file. Now Mr. Misetic is focussing on confessions. This -- only this witness could say what exactly the factors were which made him conclude that there was no reliable evidence to charge those five persons. And based on his examination, he arrived at the conclusion that there was no evidence, reliable evidence, against those five persons, not withstanding confession. I don't think, as being attorneys, we have to, you know, argue that just because there is one confession, that that suffices for an entire -- for a person to be convicted of a crime. Now, what this witness has said was that he examined the entire case material, and he arrived at that conclusion. Then he wondered as to who the real perpetrators were, upon which he initiated a further investigation, and then the Mr. Nenad Mrkota and Goran Vunic material came forward. So I do not see what the contradiction is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not focus on the contradiction. Would it be a suggestion that you put a question to the witness in relation to when he determined that there was no basis to continue that case, whether he specifically considered any confessions which were in that file. If you ask him that, as a very factual question not of a general character, then we will hear what the witness says. It might meet some of Mr. Misetic's concerns and might not be inconsistent with what you just told us. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you had two questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which means it becomes three, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I allow you the third one. But the 30 to 40 minutes you indicated yesterday, even without my permission, have now grown to one hour and 20 minutes, not all of it used for the examination of the witness, but most of it. Can the witness be brought into the courtroom again. Ms. Mahindaratne, are the other to questions related to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will make it just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please don't make it too complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, when you examined the Varivode, Gosic material and arrived at the conclusion that there was no reliable evidence to proceed against the five persons who were indicted in the previous case, did you consider the confessions made by those accused?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The confessions were a particular subject of my interest and consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Could you just explain to Court very briefly, Mr. Zganjer, because we're running out of time, what were the factors, and if could you say briefly, which made you exclude or reject those confessions as not being true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key reason for which the confessions were not accepted was the fact that what some of the accused had confessed before the investigating judge simply did not match the factual situation on the spot, as it was established in Gosic and Varivode. In other words, the accused in question, who provided their alleged confessions of their act, actually spoke about something that had nothing whatsoever to do with what had actually happened in Gosic and Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: And were those confessions made before -- I'm sorry. I repeat will it: Were those confessions made before the investigating judge or to the police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key element for me was the fact that the confessions were made before the investigating judge, when the accused were first brought in and when the accused were first examined by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. My last question to you is: Did you have any reason to doubt that Sibenik-Knin crime police officers, who were investigating the Grubori event, were not reporting the information they were collecting accurately to you, regarding the particular investigation? I'm referring to the Grubori event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a linguistic matter, you asked whether the witness had any reason to doubt that the events were not reported correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you wanted to say, with any reason to believe that they did not report it correctly or whether you had any doubt as to whether the reporting was in accordance with the information they disposed of?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With this clarification, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no reason for me to doubt that after I had instigated criminal investigation procedure, the police officer involved in the investigation would misinform me. I believe that the police officers, at the time, six years after the event, acting on my request, did everything that was objectively possible at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARANTE
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief. I apologise for the extra time I took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will first have a break. Could I verify with the Defence counsel the timing now in relation to what you now from the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will be the first one to cross-examine the witness, and I can predict, let's say, four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four hours. Mr. Misetic, are you the second one or it Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is unlikely that we will have any questions at all, but it really depends on what my learned friend covers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No more than one and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which makes it five and a half hours. The Chamber will consider the time requested. We'll first have a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, if in your mind you would reduce the time, then there's a fair chance that it turns out to be less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think it is more or less the usual procedure, Your Honour. I will try to use less time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean you will try not to lose yourself too many matters in the background of the witness and not to repeat yourself. Is that it? If you say that's what I'm going to try again, I will fully adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try and do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have minuted, I wanted to place on the record that the Prosecution tendered 65 ter 6097 through the bar table motion, and the parties have agreed that -- this is the a full judgement of D843, marked for identification. The parties have grade that the full judgement could replace the excerpt that has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Let me just check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D853, that is the partial --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Excerpt of the judgement tendered in the course of Mr. Simic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would then replaced by the judgment in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, more judgement could not harm, could it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm checking to make sure it's the right judgement. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, Ms. Mahindaratne, you will provide a list of all the bar table --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no objection to replacing it. It is the same judgement. I'm just checking. I believe we are the ones that have upload it since it is a D exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a D exhibit. Therefore, it is logical that you would upload it, if you have it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is uploaded. We just have to put in as D843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then can you upload as a -- you can't replace the D843, but Madam Registrar will replace D843 by the judgement in its entirety as will be uploaded under number --
