utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 6097 appears on the list and had provisionally been assigned Exhibit P1077 by Madam Registrar, but this will then be vacated, and we'll find this will then that we need new numbers for that. Yes, that's now on the record. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zganjer. In these proceedings, I represent General Markac, and I will you putting questions to you in that capacity. I will be mindful of the fact that much time has elapsed, and I appeal to you to answer my questions to the best of your recollection. At the same time, please bear in mind that there should be a break between question and answer, in order to enable the interpreters to do their job. Mr. Zganjer, in the state attorney's office previously that was the prosecutor's office, you have spent some 28 years in all, and I will not be wrong if I say that you have a great many experience in the field of the administration of justice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Nowadays in the Republic of Croatia, in the justice administration, do there exist special military courts and special military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no military courts and military prosecutor's office today within the justice administration system in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, in the period covered by the indictment, more precisely I mean the second half of 1995, there existed both military courts and a military prosecutor's office, did there not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These judiciary bodies were set up pursuant to or by virtue of the powers of the president of the Republic and by virtue of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, when, in 1991 a decree was passed on the organisation work and the scope of work of the judiciary. I will show you the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 3D01-0576. [In English] Your Honour, what we will see in course of my cross-examination, and that includes this very document, is a partial translation of the document that has been provided by the Defence. Meanwhile, while we are waiting for the official translation that has been demanded a few times ago, I would like to stress that preparing for the cross-examination, I realized a quite important mistake in translation, and I would like to stress upon it; that is, that mistake relates to the translation of the Croatian words "vojni sud," which is "military court." In our wrong translation, that has been translated as "court martial," which is not exactly the very same definition, because according to the Black's Law Dictionary, the court martial is an ad hoc military court under military authority, to try and punish those who violated the code of military justice, and it's not part of the judiciary system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that in the statement given by this witness that the term "court martial" has caused a few problems. Although I always prefer to say that you have second thoughts as far as the translation is concerned or not, because finally our translators are the professionals who assist us in doing the job, but, of course, there's no problem whatsoever to share your thinking with them, and each the word "vojni sud" sounds familiar in my ears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to cover this topic through the cross-examination with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zganjer, you see on the screen the decree on the organisation work and the domain of the judiciary in the case of war. Are you familiar with this decree?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that this is an extraordinary legal instrument or an emergency legal instrument provoked by the state of war and the war situation in 1991 in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can fully agree on that. This is something the very title of the decree indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to Article 2, which stipulates the establishment of the military court. In Article 6, the jurisdiction of the military courts is laid down. Let us turn to the second page of the decree, and look at Article 7 and Article 8. There, it is provided that the district courts should decide appeals against the decisions of military courts, and that, as a last instance, the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia shall hear the appeals from the decisions rendered by military courts. Do you agree, Mr. Zganjer, that it follows from this decree that the supervision of the military court was exercised by the civilian judiciary?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 11 of the decree states that the presidents and judges of the military courts shall, by war assignment, be appointed by the minister of defence at the proposal of the minister of justice and administration from among the judges of municipal and district courts. Please tell us something more about this. Where were military judges recruited from, the ones who sat on the newly established military courts in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military courts were manned from the ranks of the judges who, up until the adoption of this decree, served as judges in regular courts; that's to say, in the municipal courts and in the district or county courts in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there special training or professional advancement organised for the judges who were transferred from civilian courts to the military courts, in view of the application of law and procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, these judges did not undergo any special training. They continued performing practically the same duties whilst applying the jurisdiction prescribed by this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that the military courts applied the same Criminal Code and same Law on Criminal Procedure that applied by civilian courts? In other words, there did not exist any special regulations governing procedure before military courts.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Military courts applied the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code. At the time, it was the General Criminal Code of the Republic of Croatia, later to become the Criminal Code of the Republic of Croatia. In other words, they applied the same legal provisions as were applied by judges of the regular civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the jurisdiction of military courts. We can speak of a three-fold jurisdiction: Territorial, subject matter jurisdiction, and temporal jurisdiction. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject matter jurisdiction of military courts transpires from Article 2 of this decree, unless I'm mistaken. As for the territorial jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of military courts was specific insofar as the territorial jurisdiction was defined according to the area covered by a given military district. Let me be quite specific. For instance, the military court in Split covered the area from Zadar all the way to Dubrovnik. For the crimes within the purview of military courts, that was the only court that had jurisdiction over that. In order to rationalise the procedure, the judges from the military court in Split would, to make proceedings easier, go to Sibenik or Zadar to hear cases, although the court which had jurisdiction was the one in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we take this to be a practical relocation of proceedings to make the conduct of proceedings more practical?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please, to turn back one page and focus on Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Military courts were authorised to hear cases, as we see in Article 6, perpetrators for crimes if the perpetrators were active servicemen. So there was no dispute there. If it was established that the perpetrator was a military serviceman, then that person would be tried before a military court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, can you recall that regard to the subject matter jurisdiction, still there was some problems because some accused had perpetrated crimes in military uniforms and presented themselves as members of a military unit, although they were not members of any military units, and then the subject matter jurisdiction of a military court would come into question.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, while I worked in the military prosecutor's office, there were very few such cases, or at least there are very few in the cases that I dealt with. At this moment, I can't remember any particular case where the subject matter jurisdiction would come into question. We're talking about the years 1992 and 1993, and it would be very much the question of the qualification of the person who appeared before the military court, but that was very seldom in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the subject matter jurisdiction. Military courts were authorised to try civilian persons, were they not, in some very specific and legally prescribed cases? For example, if a civilian committed a crime against a military [indiscernible] or official duty, or if a civilian committed a crime in concert with servicemen so on and so forth. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D906.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D906 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Given the provisions of Article 11 of the decree that we just saw, I would kindly ask the registry to display document number 3D01-0574.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to come up, let me tell you that we're going to see a decision on the assignment of a judge in the military court in Split and the abolishment of that position, to illustrate the implementation of Article 11 of the decree. We will see that the decision is dated 10 August 1995, and that it was issued by the then-minister of defence, Gojko Susak, pursuant to the Article 11 of the decree that we just saw, and upon the proposal by the minister of justice of the Republic of Croatia. The judges of the military court in Split were reassigned and became judges of the municipal court in Split, and the subject of this decision or solution is the postings and appeal of the war postings of the judges. Could you please explain to the Judges what this is about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the matter that you have just explained. This is a solution on the postings and appeal of the war postings of the judges. I received an almost identical decision when I was appointed with a decision of the deputy judge of the military court, and this was decided by the then-minister of defence, Gojko Susak, upon a proposal by the minister of justice. This was our war assignment in the statement of war or immediate -- an immediate threat of war, and this assignment was carried out pursuant to the decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't appear on the transcript that you wanted to tender this document, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D907.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D907 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] May the Court please produce 3D01-0580.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will shortly see a document which is the Law on Courts issued in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mistake in typing the document, where it says that it is from 6th of January 1984. It has to be 1994, as it properly has been written in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Law on Courts and I would like to draw your attention to Articles 5 and 6, which we will shortly see on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in these Articles that courts will try cases based on the constitution and the laws, as well as the international laws that are part of rule of law of the Republic of Croatia. Article 6 strictly forbids any influence on judicial decisions. Article 13 mentions the courts that are envisaged by the law as existing in the Republic of Croatia, and it also says that military courts are established as per Article 14 for a certain number of cases. Article 18 speaks about the jurisdiction of the aforementioned military courts. This document, i.e., the Law on Courts, regulates the matters of military courts at the time that we're talking about, which is in the year 1995; would you agree Mr., Zganjer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number D908.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D908 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, earlier, when you quoted from where the judges would be recruited, you read and you quoted "municipal and county courts."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not what the text we had on the screen at the time said. So I wondered whether that was a follow-up situation that perhaps, at a later stage, that included county courts as well; and since we have now in Article 14 again municipal courts and county courts, I'm just seeking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I quoted this from Article 11 of the decree from 1991, where it stated that: "From among the judges of municipal courts ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you read "county courts" as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is written in the original; and by our mistake, that hasn't been translated. I apologise again, and we will have the proper translation as soon as we receive it from the official translating services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, and apologies for getting back to it so late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have a very sharp eye, I must say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, within the military organisation, Mr. Zganjer, there was a certain structure that processed perpetrators of disciplinary offences committed by members of the military; wouldn't that be the case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Those were military disciplinary courts as we used to call them.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also military disciplinary prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The position and definition of those bodies was something that relied exclusively on the military structure.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I believe that the bodies were established sometime in 1995 or 1996, but I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the military disciplinary courts did not have jurisdiction to process perpetrators of crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: They were not under the control of the civilian authorities, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you say something about the following situation: Let's say, for example, that a soldier or a military serviceman who were to be processed for a crime, and if a sentence was passed for that crime, would disciplinary proceedings be carried out before a military disciplinary court despite the fact that that person is already being tried for a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that proceedings before a military courts for a crime in a certain way enveloped any possible military disciplinary responsibility of a serviceman. In concrete terms, this would mean, if I'm not mistaken, if a person was found guilty and sentenced for a crime, then this would have enveloped that same person's responsibility for a possible disciplinary offence. In the category of crimes, a crime is the highest form of a punishable act and, therefore, it is higher in the hierarchy than a disciplinary offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's try and explain that on a rather simple example. A soldier or a serviceman gets drunk in a local pub and causes disturbance; and, by that, he commits a disciplinary offence under the jurisdiction of a disciplinary military court. However, let's go one step further. That same person, a drunken soldier, during his misbehaviour uses a fire-arm and kills a person. Criminal proceedings are thus instigated against that person before a military court. Will that person be prosecuted for a disciplinary offence and for a crime, or whether he would only be processed for a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be only for a crime, either for a murder or an attempted murder, and that the decision of the military court, if we're talking about that time, will envelope or consume the same person's military disciplinary responsibility. If you will allow me, I would like to say something else. If the military court were to find that person guilty of a crime -- of murder or attempted murder, I allow myself to assume that that person would be dishonourably discharged from the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank you for this explanation. In your interview to the investigators of the OTP, you said that the military courts were not involved in the proceedings for war crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was prescribed by the regulations that were in effect at that time in the Republic of Croatia. I wouldn't really go into the assumptions as to why this existed in the law, and I don't think it would be of any use to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Zganjer: Regular courts were the ones trying cases of war crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Croatian criminal law that was in effect at the time, the definition of a war crime was, to a certain extent, different than in the Statute of this court or in the current legislations of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the relevant time, the compositions of the provisions of the criminal legislation that covered war crimes was completely different than it is today, and it also differed greatly from what has been envisaged by the documents of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am particularly underlining the term "command responsibility." Could you please tell us how was this term "command responsibility" defined in the then-Croatian legislation, and how could one be processed for crimes on the basis of this institute of command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the criminal legislation of the Republic of Croatia that was in effect at the time, persons who could be tried for war crimes were those who ordered a war crime to be committed and law defined the acts of war crime in more specific terms. So it would be the person who ordered a war crime, as well as the person who committed or carried out the order to commit a war crime. So that would be that. The person giving order and the person carrying out the order, one or more of then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We know that there were several trials ongoing and against persons accused of war crimes, especially persons of Serb ethnicity, and those proceedings were mostly carried in absentia, if you will agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, especially so in the period between 1991 and 1995 or 1996. Of course, the majority of these persons of Serb ethnicity, due to the undisputable existence of an armed conflict, were out of reach of the Croatian authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the proceedings were held and the culpable person, the culprit, was sentenced, but he was out of reach. Now, how did the Law on Criminal Procedure regulate the situation where a person is found and arrested and becomes available to the justice administration? How was the trial in absentia regulated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the individual tried who was tried in absentia is found and arrested and taken into custody and forwarded to the serving of the sentence, it was sufficient for that individual to file a request for a retrial and to just write one sentence as a statement of reasons for its -- for his claim, just to write that "I was tried in absentia and I would now wish to be retried." That would be enough for the court to ask for a retrial to be tried by a new panel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, the sentence passed previously was invalidated and a retrial held where a different decision would be rendered at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. You are fully right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was where a different decision would be rendered at the end of it. What do I have to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or a different decision should be stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was invalidated. Yes, a different decision would invalidate the earlier decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was it always a different decision, or could it be the same decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It depends on the results of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the question puzzled me. You've heard what I asked. Would you agree with what was said, that the retrial could result in a different decision or in a same decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. During a retrial, the earlier verdict could be upheld; however, a retrial, where the individual tried would be present, could result in a different decision and in a different verdict where the person can be acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. We said that under the extraordinary war circumstances, the military court system was introduced. By the logic of things, what the civilian police did in respect of the civilian judiciary, that's what the military police did in relation to the military judiciary. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In fact, as you put it, the military police was created from scratch in 1991 and became gradually trained. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true and it's a fact, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that it would be fortunate if a civilian police officer was transferred to the military police because, thus, the fellow military policemen could benefit from his knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I fully stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thus, for instance, I don't know if you're aware this, the chief of the military police, Mr. Mate Lausic, was formerly a policeman who had spent a great deal of his career in the civilian police. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the start of the war in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, both the military and civilian police forces were to a considerable extent engaged in combat. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were part of the body of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In time, the civilian police increasingly withdrew from that particular function and turned to the function which it normally performs in peacetime. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as the military police concerned, there existed special anti-terrorist units which also had combat assignments within the military police system. Are aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do allow for the fact and concede the fact that this system existed within the military police structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now try to reconstruct the proceedings which was touched upon on several occasions during your examination-in-chief. I should like to approach this matter more systematically. What sort of procedure follows once the police has received a report or an account that a crime was supposedly committed, that there were suspicions. For instance, there's a phone ringing in the police station, and the person at the other end of the line says that there's a body found there that could be the result of murder. What is the police duty-bound to do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once such a report has been received, the policemen working in the operative centre of the police administration will attempt to collect, gather certain information from the individuals who can provide that information, where the body is, in which area. That particular operative centre officer will make a note of the information, whereupon he will notify the duty officer within the crime police force thereof. The crime police will then inform the duty state attorney and the duty investigating judge of the report. The investigating judge will learn from that particular police officer what the case involved; and, on the basis of that, he will decide whether to attend the scene or whether to leave the scene of crime investigation down to the police. This sort of experience indicates that in all of more serious cases, as was the one that we took as a case in point, the investigating judge always attended the scene and personally conducted the crime of scene investigation. Always in such cases, the duty state attorney would attend the scene together with the duty investigating judge. That would be the procedure, roughly, upon receipt of such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to clarify further the procedure. You said that the investigating judge would attend the scene to examine the crime of scene, together with the duty state attorney. Would the investigating judge, where there was a suspected murder involved, make sure that the scene of crime investigation team included other individuals who had specialist knowledge in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the team who had to, without fail, attend and take part in such an examination of the scene crime, were members of the forensic team of the police administration; in other words, persons who were specially trained to collect all the valuable trace evidence that can be obtained at a scene, in order to subject the evidence to the appropriate forensic analysis and examination, expertise. It was not unusual for a physician or a coroner to attend the scene as well, in order to ascertain the fact the death. With a cursory external examination of the body, he would indicate the mechanism or the manner of death. He would be able to tell if the person died of natural or violent causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, a final decision on the mechanism and cause of injury or death could be made, in the case of death, once a post-mortem is done. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was the person authorised to order that an autopsy be conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Croatian law, only the investigating judge could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that members of the crime of scene investigation team had to be, and they would be asked for by the investigating judge, members of the forensic team, who would then collect the evidence necessary for possible further prosecution. Who was responsible to secure the trace evidence and the scene, once such a report has been received, to make sure that no contamination of the evidence takes place before the arrival of the forensic team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police officer who answered the phone and received the information that a dead body was found somewhere would, even before conveying that information to the duty officer of the crime police, order the police patrol in charge of that particular area to urgently go to the crime scene, to secure it, to cordon it off, to make sure that it was barred to anyone, all it, of course, it make sure that the trace evidence remains preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your practice, did you have the experience of attending a crime scene with your associates that had not been secured by members of the general duty police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely, very rarely. Because by the nature of things, before the arrival of the duty investigating judge and duty state attorney, there would always be the police already there, securing the scene. However, in my many years of practice, I am aware of the cases, admittedly not that many, where the duty judge and state attorney would be there before the police themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But these were exceptions, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. To your recollection, how many investigating judges were there, in all, in the Sibenik area and in the Zadar area at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sibenik investigating centre, as far as I remember, during the war - in other words, between 1992 and 1995 - there were three to four investigating judges, I believe. I can't speak about Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the investigating centre or the investigation centre. Can you briefly explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what sort of an organisation is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation centre was, in organisational terms, a part of the county or district court, employing investigating judges in charge of acting in the cases we've just referred to, as well as in charge of the investigation carried out against a person or more persons who are suspected perpetrators of an act. I stress that primarily these were judges who were within the court system assigned to the duties of investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These would primarily or exclusively be the judges of the county courts, or rather, district courts at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were judges of the county or district courts who conducted investigations, both in the cases that came under the jurisdiction of the county or district court and of the municipal court. In other words, this work was focussed in the -- or concentrated in the investigative branch of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In order for the judges to be able to be assigned to a county court, they had to have a certain degree of professional experience.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the power of the president of the court was such that he was able to assign judges to various divisions, be it investigations, trials, or appeals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the relationship between a judge - in this case, an investigating judge - and a public prosecutor or a state attorney? What was their relationship? If we're looking at a hierarchy, would judges be under the jurisdiction or the state attorney which used to be public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigating judge, as a judge, was obviously independent and acted on his or her own, and he was under no jurisdiction or authority of the state attorney. During an on-site investigation, he was the one who called the shots, to put it that way. Everything that was done at the scene could only be done on the order of an investigating judge. The task or the function of the public prosecutor who attended the on-site inspection was to provide suggestions or proposals to the judge as to what would be good to do at that particular moment, but the final decision was in the hands of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, a prosecutor, i.e., the state attorney, had certain authorities or powers over the police. Could you explain that relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the on-site inspection was finished, the investigating judge would submit his record on the on-site inspection to the state attorney. From then on, the proceedings would be channelled towards the detection of the perpetrator of the given crime, towards collecting evidence; and this was a matter of a coordinator -- a coordinating activity involving the public prosecutor and the police. In this stage of pre-criminal proceedings, the judge did not have any say, i.e., did not get involved in this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have also mentioned the record on the on-site inspection which, by its nature, would be a document that would be used in the future proceedings, in terms of establishing the situation that was found on site. In probative terms, this record was a valid document and could be used as evidence in the future trial. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was a very valuable piece of evidence in a future trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In a situation when the investigating judge handed over the on-site inspection to the police, and when he would not be present in person together with the public prosecutor during the on-site investigation, it would be the police that made a note of the inspection.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the probative value on the record of the onsite inspection made by the police, would it be the same as the one made by the judge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The probative value would still be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers so far. When we're talking about the investigating centre and the function of the investigating judge, the investigating centre was operating around the clock. Is that correct? There was always somebody on duty.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can testify to the way how it was organised in Sibenik. For example, in Sibenik, the duty service lasted for seven days, so one judge would be on duty for seven days together with a prosecutor. But it depended on the amount of work and the intensity of the criminal activity, which differs from one territory to another, from one region to another. It is certain that a lot more is happening in Zagreb than what is happening in Sibenik. Given the size of the city, it goes without saying that the two are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. In a way, you have answered my next question, and the question would be whether the -- a representative of the state attorney's office would be on duty together with the judge, and you have already told us that that was the case. An investigating judge on his part and a prosecutor on his part also had to make their entries in the so-called duty log-book. Could you tell us something about that log-book, how it was established and what was entered in the log-book by the two people on duty?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you more details in answering this question if I speak about the tasks of the state attorney. A state attorney, who was on duty together with an investigating judge and who would go to the scene of crime and attend an on-site inspection, when he returned to his office, he had to make his short comments in the so-called duty log-book. He had to say where he went, when he went there, he had to leave a written trace of his on-site inspection. The final document was the investigating judge's note on the on-site inspection that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have already mentioned a case where, for example, a body was found, an on-site inspection was carried out, and the investigating judge attending the on-site inspection would order the body to be taken to the morgue -- to a morgue for autopsy. Are you aware of a case when a judge would not be involved in an on-site inspection involving a dead body, and what would the procedure? I'm here referring to the "asanacija" or the clean-up of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigating judge would have to go to the site if he received a report on a dead body; however, this procedure called "asanacija" or clean-up is somewhat different. I'm not an expert, and I can't really talk about that. But as an informed layperson, I may be able to provide some suggestions as to the procedure called "asanacija." This clean-up or "asanacija" is carried out in the following way: Dead bodies are removed from a certain area in order to preserve those bodies in their integral form and prevent them from being mutilated by animals and prevent any spreading of diseases of course. However, this procedure, "asanacija" or clean-up, basically boiled down to a somewhat shorter piece of information as to where the body was found, and the further procedure with the body was to record the position of the body by a photo or a video-clip. But in that, one would record that part of the body or the characteristics of the body that might be used for the identification of the body on the part of their next of kin. After the "asanacija" or the clean-up of the body, that body was buried in a certain place, and a record was made of the fact where the body was found in a certain place and, finally, where it would be buried. That would be the long and short of this pre-record called "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the procedure called "asanacija" is much different from the procedure called an on-site inspection that you have described for us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about two completely different procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that "asanacija" was carried out within the structure of the Ministry of Interior and that the judiciary did not get involved in this procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about the experiences I had in Sibenik. I suppose my learned friend, when you're talking about "asanacija" and you're asking me about it, you probably referring to the events that followed a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I meant, and I apologise if I was not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence of Sibenik and in the territory under the jurisdiction of the Sibenik judiciary, there were procedures of "asanacija." An investigating judge was not on site in every such case. However, when he received a report from the police that a body was discovered during an "asanacija," he would issue an order for these bodies, before they were buried, to be autopsied in the Sibenik hospital by a forensic pathologist, so as to establish, by the external examination of the body, the time of death, the cause of death, and the mechanism of the onset of any injuries. I know that this was done by the investigating judge in Sibenik, that the bodies were brought to the morgue, and that the forensic pathologist did carry out an external examination of the bodies. There is a written trace to that effect both in the investigating office of -- the office of the investigating judge in Sibenik, as well as in the Sibenik hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you cannot speak with any certainty about the territory under the jurisdiction of the Zadar county court?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can't tell you anything very precise about the territory under the jurisdiction of the Zadar court, but what I can tell you, because it is a fact, in territorial terms, the area of Zadar and Knin county was much larger than the territory of the Sibenik county. We're talking about the time following the military and police operation Oluja. The territory of the Zadar and Knin county was much larger than the territory of the Sibenik county, and I believe that this fact had a major impact on the procedure of "asanacija" in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This answer of yours brings us to the topic of issues that existed at the time, and I'm primarily referring to the events that followed Oluja in 1995, in the month of August, September, October, November, and December. This was a large territory, and you've already told us what the number of judges there was. In any case, there was a shortage of staff that could adequately respond to every report and act in keeping with legal and technical requirements. Could you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For example, if a duty investigating judge received a report that there was a suspicion death in the territory of a village and he went to carry out an on-site inspection, and, at the same time, a report was received that maybe half an hour or an hour later a similar thing had happened in a different village a bit further from the first one, how is that conflicted situation involved? Obviously, an investigating judge could not be in the two places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the only way possible: The investigating judge would be involved in an on-site inspection where he found himself at the moment when the report was received, and he would leave the "asanacija" or the on-site inspection to the police officials in the place for which he received the subsequent report, the report on a dead body, because objectively he could not be in two different places at the same time. Very often, these two places would be at a very long distance from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this was not something that was not very common at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your interview with the investigators of the OTP of this Tribunal, you also spoke about the technical elements of criminal proceedings. You mentioned DNA samples and DNA analysis as well. In the modern world, the two are in common use. Let's go back to the year 1995. What are your recollections with regard to the technical compatibilities of the then-police force and the investigating judges when it came to the scientific methods that you were used then and comparing them with the modern methods used today?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of us in 1995 were aware of the DNA analysis; however, in everyday police work, that methodology of the collection of valuable and unquestionable evidence was not used. It was only a bit later that we could employ trained people and all the necessary technology. Today, as a result of that, the Croatian DNA centre - let me call it that way because I don't know its proper name - is housed in the hospital in Zadar. It is one of the most respectable DNA centres in the territory of Balkan and wider area. But at the same time, the DNA analysis was not in use in the police proceedings when it came to the collection of valuable traces and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There's another problem that you touched upon in your interview with the OTP, which was the problem of a large number of unregistered weaponry present at the time. Can you tell us briefly what the problem involved?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a malignant problem at the time, a problem that the Republic of Croatia is faced with even today and has been trying to resolve it. From the start of the homeland war, as our armed forces were in the making, there must have been oversights and errors made in the process of issuing individuals with weapons and making sure that they are returned. As the war neared its end, as Croatia was liberated, members of the public were also able to get hold of weapons. At the time, there was a high fluctuation of weapons that changed hands. It was a serious problem then and is a serious problem now in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I have in mind - and I'm perhaps suggesting the answer there - is that at one scene of an incident, bullet casings were found. Would it be possible to apply certain procedures to find out what sort of weapon the bullets were fired from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The best solution would have been for the bullet casings to be immediately collected from the scene when the body was found, because what happened in the meantime with the casings remaining there? They were exposed to the natural extremities, they rusted, and once they were found three, four, five, years later, their reliability would be highly questionable in terms of a ballistic examination to determine which rifle they were fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I intervene for one second. Apparently, Mr. Mikulicic, you're raising the issue that if there is an lot of weaponry around which is not registered, that it might be rather difficult to find a weapon for inspection, whether it matches with the bullet casings found. That is clear even without putting a question to the witness. I mean, if there is it no proper registration, it is difficult. Even without the proper registration, it is also difficult, unless you have all the characterize of each weapon stored in a central system, which was not the case. Of course, we earlier heard about that if you know that there is a limited number of people in a certain area where it's registered what weaponry they have used, that at least you have a limited number of weapons that you could use to see whether they match. That's all clear. So, apparently, you wanted to raise this issue. That's at least how I understand your question. And from my observations now, it may be clear to you that you don't have to go through every step with the Bench of trained and professional Judges. Apart from that, the matter has been raised several times already in this case. Now, the witness starts answering on a totally different subject; that is, that if the bullet casings are exposed to whether conditions, then the quality may diminish. You just let the witness go explaining a matter which was totally not what you apparently were seeking. So, therefore, if you would keep better control over, first of all, what we need to know and what is not yet there in evidence and what is not yet therefore, I would say often, obvious, if you would focus on that first. Then, second, if the witness goes in a totally different direction, if you would stop him for a second and say, "Well, I was not talking about the quality of the material found, but I was talking about a different thing," then we would certainly proceed more quickly. I'm looking at the clock. I have one or two additional questions for the witness. Mr. Zganjer, in one question, you were asked about the relationship between the state attorney and the investigating judge. Could an investigating judge become active without a state attorney triggering, initiating this activity? Was the investigating judge dependent on the initiative taken by the state attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigating judge becomes fully involved from the point when the state attorney files an investigating request before him against a person in respect of which there are reasons to suspect that the person involved committed a crime. This was a stage in the proceedings; and under the Croatian law, that is what is properly termed "the investigation." In the pre-criminal proceedings, the activities aimed at identifying the perpetrator of a crime and gathering high-quality evidence lay exclusively within the purview of the police and the investigating judge. In this stage, the investigating judge decides upon certain investigating actions that may constitute an encroachment upon the rights of the citizens. In other words, in the pre-criminal proceedings or in the pre-criminal stage of the proceedings, only the investigating judge can allow that somebody's home is searched, with a view to ensuring that the police and the state attorney may find helpful evidence in this particular residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you explained for what activities an investigating judge was needed. What I'd like to know is: Could an investigating judge, on his own initiative or on the initiative of the police, but without the intervention of the state attorney, for example, during crime scene investigation; or was he dependent the initiative taken by the state attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If an investigation has been launched and it is led by the investigating judge and there was no on-site inspection, the investigating judge can carry this out on his own autonomous decision. In the pre-criminal stage of the proceedings, the investigating judge decides whether to carry out an on-site investigation or whether to get involved in an on-site inspection, if the police informs him that a body has been found in a certain location. It is then that the judge makes a decision, goes to the site, and he is then the person who is immediately involved in the investigation by carrying out, by leading an on-site inspection. However, I would like to add something to your question, if I may. In the pre-criminal stage of the proceedings, the issue of the detection of a perpetrator and collection of quality evidence is not a primary interest of the investigating judge. It is primarily the interests of the police and the state attorney who gives his quality contribution in this stage of the procedure. This stage of the procedure is not of special interest of the investigating judge. He expects other bodies to submit to him all the quality evidence and the request to instigate criminal proceedings against a certain person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that in the pre-criminal investigations, that the activity of the investigating judge can be triggered merely by being informed by the police. If you would disagree, I would like to hear. Mr. Mikulicic, I have another matter. You warned us -- but perhaps I should first pay proper attention to whether the witness disagrees or not. I should give him an opportunity to explain or otherwise. If you'd like to think it over, my question, then we would come back to it tomorrow, Mr. Zganjer. We are a bit under time pressure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree with you, Honourable Judge, that, in the pre-criminal stage of the proceedings, an investigating judge make decisions on going to the site of the crime upon having received a police report that something extraordinary had happened in a certain place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, one issue. On P906 -- no, I should say D906, you warned us -- that is the decree on the organisation and the work and the domain of the judiciary in case of war. You warned us about translation issues. Now, looking at D908 which is the Law on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... situation is concerning all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that is it understood, because I noticed that court martials are found there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... mistake of the translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
